newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Germany exudes renewed EMU vigour at ECOFIN talks.
newsitem.headline: Germany exudes renewed EMU vigour at ECOFIN talks.

text.p: Germany displayed renewed vigour in its battle to qualify for monetary union this weekend, strengthened in its efforts by an injection of political dynamism from Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

Kohl's decision to run again in a general election that must be held next year, and to link the decision clearly to the need to make the European Union's planned single currency a success, was welcomed universally by EU finance ministers meeting in the seaside town of Noordwijk.

Within the German delegation, Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer both exuded confidence in the stability of the planned single currency as a scheme to ensure a tight budget spending by EMU nations was approved.
And Waigel quashed talk that Germany itself -- seen as an essential EMU member -- might fail to meet the stringent economic entry conditions set for monetary union.
"There is no change on that -- we will meet the criteria," he told reporters after talks with his European counterparts.

Germany's position as Europe's largest economy, with Europe's longest serving government leader at its helm, means that confidence in the entire region's ability to create a single currency in 1999 can rise and fall with Germany's fate.

Shock German jobless figures at the start of this year gave strength to so-called Eurosceptics by casting doubt on Germany's ability to rein in its budget spending to three percent of gross domestic product, the level set in the EU's Maastricht Treaty.

Some improved economic data has given hope recently that the government's target of 2.9 percent may be less out of reach than first thought, but the jury is still out on whether jobless queues will reduce, as forecast, by mid-year.

Yet the pendulum of European sentiment swung straight back into positive territory late last week, with Kohl's decision to throw his considerable political clout behind monetary union by pledging to stand again as chancellor in autumn 1998 polls.
The decision was widely seen as the best possible way to demonstrate that Germany's political drive toward monetary union -- which some had believed was faltering -- was intact.
"Chancellor Kohl is one of the greatest European politicians with a very clear vision of the future of Europe," Danish Finance Minister Marianne Jelved told Reuters.
"If anyone still had any doubts about European monetary union starting on time they have no ground for those doubts now," she added.
But Germany nonetheless faces difficult months ahead.

Data due in May on the estimated tax income for 1997 is seen by many as a watershed which will decide whether there is any chance of Germany cutting its deficit to the three percent maximum this year, the crunch year for EMU qualification.

Although Germany could try to argue a special case for its excessive deficit, as it has on its high debt level, due to the huge budgetary strain of German unification, domestically such an argument could prove a political minefield.

The inflation-conscious German public, educated by repeated statements from political heavyweights -- including Waigel himself -- that the Maastricht budget goal is a maximum of 3.0 percent, would find a sudden change of view hard to swallow. That could in turn lead for calls for a delay to the EMU start.
"If the tax estimate shows a considerable shortfall the door will really be opened to rumours of delay," Ulrike Kastens, analyst at Trinkaus Capital Management said.

Waigel to some extent left his options open in Noordwijk, declining to be drawn either on the precise definition of the Maastricht budget deficit criteria or on legal possibilities to delay the 1999 start of the single currency.
"Three is three," he repeated on the budget goals, dodging questions as to whether 3.2 could be close enough.

On the issue of delay, which Germany has repeatedly said is not being considered, he commented, "We had no discussion of that at all...If I have a view on it I will not express it. A news conference also gives the opportunity not to say some things."
